### Security tracking repository

Douglas reported that the private [`security-tracking`](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/security-tracking) repository is up and mirroring security advisories. He has been using it to organize his work on the LMS/HSS reports, but has not seen anyone else use it, and asked whether others find it useful. Rodrigo does: not every TSC member is a maintainer everywhere, so this is the only place they can see all open advisories and group related ones. He will also look into a separate access question raised the previous week, where Norm lacked access to some of the repositories where fixes are being developed.

Michael, struck by the length of the list, asked how and by whom it is being worked. Douglas explained that the previously discussed "quarterback" process is not being followed and triage is ad hoc — he and Bruce went over the list in their prioritization meeting this week, with Bruce taking on a couple of items and Douglas working the LMS/HSS ones — but there is no systematic process. Rodrigo argued the length of the list is not entirely within OQS's control: many advisories concern algorithms OQS does not maintain, and he cited an open CROSS issue that the CROSS team has never been told about, making it impossible for them to act. Most current items are LMS/XMSS, which Cisco is responsible for, but that will not always be the case; OQS's own responsibility is to notify the parties who committed to supporting each implementation — the role the quarterback model was meant to fill.

Logan, attending as a non-member and without access to the repository, described the reporting side: a local LLM run over SLH-DSA surfaced an issue that he took to the upstream maintainer via Discord, who merged the fix, and he keeps direct contacts on submission teams (e.g. for Kyber) so he has someone to ask. His point was that LLM-assisted and manual audits will keep producing findings, and what is missing is a defined escalation path to the upstream algorithm teams.

Michael proposed collecting GitHub handles alongside emails and tagging the responsible person on the GitHub security advisory itself. Rodrigo objected that non-maintainers cannot see the tracking repository, but Douglas confirmed that individuals can be invited to individual advisories submitted through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, even though they cannot be invited to tracking-repository issues. The real work and the interaction with the reporter would therefore happen on the advisory, with the tracking repository recording that upstream has been notified; Michael had already done this once by tagging Norm on an LMS/XMSS report. The group agreed a reliable notification path is critical and that the choice of mechanism should be settled in an issue.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Open an issue to decide how responsible parties are notified of security reports (automated email to the recorded contact vs. inviting/tagging them on the GitHub security advisory), and establish the resulting procedure.

## What to do with subprojects which lose their last maintainer

Rodrigo framed the [discussion](https://github.com/open-quantum-safe/tsc/discussions/221), originally opened by Michael, around two problems: documenting that a subproject has no active maintenance, and handling incoming PRs during that period. On the first, every subproject should have a GOVERNANCE.md regardless of status, and that file is where the absence of active maintenance is stated. On the second, following Michael's straw man, the TSC chair could nominate someone — confirmed by a TSC vote — to approve and merge PRs on an unmaintained subproject, with responsibilities documented narrowly enough that it is clearly not a maintainer role; if someone later wants to become a real maintainer, they present themselves to the TSC, are voted on as usual, and the interim role ends.

Michael disliked the label "acting maintainer" and questioned whether someone without real knowledge of a subproject should be merging code; he suggested calling it *administration* rather than maintenance, being explicit to the outside world about what that means, and placing no maintainer-like obligations on the person. He argued a current AI is better placed than an uninformed human to judge such changes, and that supervised — emphatically not unsupervised — AI assistance should be an explicit part of the activity. Douglas noted this is already what he does for liboqs-python and liboqs-go, under the term "maintainer of last resort": not an AI acting alone, but a human applying a smell test to what the AI proposes (with JP's help on the Go side, and the hope that he eventually takes it over).

The group converged on the substance and, at Douglas's suggestion, on the word **caretaker**: nominated by the TSC chair, voted on by the TSC, with a narrow and clearly documented set of responsibilities, explicitly not implying active maintenance, and ending when a true maintainer is voted in.

As a concrete next step, Michael suggested starting with GOVERNANCE.md files for liboqs-go and liboqs-python and duplicating from there. Rodrigo intends to create them for every repository, but agreed to settle the language on those first; he is also writing up formal wording for the caretaker process to put to a TSC vote, which he plans to do during August (he is on vacation from Friday). Douglas noted he has a PR open in the TSC repository requesting caretaker status on liboqs-go and asked for a second review, while acknowledging the TSC could reasonably wait until the process is established.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Draft GOVERNANCE.md files documenting maintenance status — starting with liboqs-go and liboqs-python as the agreed examples — and replicate across all subprojects once the language is settled.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** Write up the caretaker role formally (nomination by the chair, TSC vote, narrow documented responsibilities, ending when a maintainer is voted in) and put it to a TSC vote during August.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (TSC members):** Review Douglas's open PR in the TSC repository requesting caretaker / maintainer-of-last-resort status on liboqs-go.

## Round 3 on-ramp

Rodrigo reported that the NIST round 3 submission deadline has moved from this Friday to August 31, giving the teams more time for final tweaks. One of the algorithms is no longer in the competition, leaving four still to be included in liboqs, and all submission teams have now responded that they are willing to help with inclusion.

**September planning.** Once the deadline has passed, Rodrigo will contact the teams to agree a date — ideally in the last week of September — for a workshop bringing them together, run along the lines of the HQC session: walking through the OQS inclusion process, hearing what they see as sticking points, and mapping out the work.

**`copy_from_upstream` refactor (Bruce).** Bruce is refactoring `copy_from_upstream` with Douglas to make it easier for upstream developers to get their source into liboqs, targeting a PR ready for review by the week before August 24, when he and Douglas attend Selected Areas in Cryptography; a co-op student joining the University of Waterloo in early September will help put the improved tool through its paces.

Asked by Michael about scope, Bruce explained that the bulk of it is removing legacy assumptions inherited from PQClean. The script assumed PQClean would be the primary source of implementations, with special cases bolted on for anything else; the accumulated "if not PQClean, do something special" branches have clogged the Python code, alongside poorly documented metadata fields whose purpose and usage are hard to trace. The refactor drops that assumption and treats essentially all implementations as standalone silos of source that compile into their own objects and then into the library.

Basil asked whether the refactor is backwards compatible for algorithms already using `copy_from_upstream` without coming from PQClean. Strictly it is not, since the metadata data sheet schema changes — some fields are renamed and the YAML structure differs — but Bruce set out three cases:

1. **A brand-new algorithm** (e.g. SDitH) simply starts on the new version of everything.
2. **A project with an active team** (e.g. mlkem-native, mldsa-native) migrates by coordination: the old `copy_from_upstream` keeps running until the new one fully replaces it, and the team then refreshes its metadata data sheet via a PR, after which it looks as though the legacy path never existed.
3. **A project with no active team** falls back to an escape hatch: `copy_from_upstream` already supports applying a liboqs-owned git patch to an upstream repository — as is done for libjade, whose upstream metadata is very incomplete — so the new schema can be applied by patch.

Basil is already preparing the SQIsign inclusion with `meta.yaml` files and the current `copy_from_upstream`, so it can be pulled into liboqs soon after publication, and asked whether that work would survive. Bruce would not promise specifics but advised not to hold his breath waiting for v2: merge with the existing tooling and migrate afterwards. The same applies to the round 2 candidates already in liboqs; Bruce offered to raise those migration PRs himself, keeping the changes minimal and readable, since he is not rewriting from scratch.

Michael asked whether the refactor changes the data structures `copy_from_upstream` emits. It does not — so, as Michael summarized and Bruce confirmed, projects happy with the old tooling can keep using it and cut over gradually rather than in one go, though the end goal is to get everybody off the legacy path.

**HQC and Falcon / FN-DSA.** Separately from the round 3 algorithms, Rodrigo will touch base again with the HQC team — last spoken to around the end of May — now that the draft standard is being prepared, to check on their inclusion plans. Douglas and Rodrigo have also been talking to Thomas Pornin, lead developer of Falcon / FN-DSA, who has agreed to join the OQS status meeting on September 1 to share updates and help OQS plan around them.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Bruce):** Have the refactored `copy_from_upstream` PR ready for review by the week before August 24.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Action (Rodrigo):** After the August 31 deadline, contact the submission teams to schedule the inclusion workshop, ideally in the last week of September.
